scenarios.title: Why a sigma-algebra?
scenarios.situation: A junior analyst says probability is simple: assign every event a number between 0 and 1 that sums to 1. Your team models continuous asset prices, so the sample space is the real line — uncountably many outcomes, with events like 'the price lands in [100, 105)' that must combine under unions and complements.
scenarios.prompt: Why can't we just define probability on EVERY subset of the real line?
choices: A sigma-algebra (closed under complements and countable unions) is required for the probability axioms to hold consistently; on an uncountable space, no assignment of probabilities to every subset satisfies countable additivity — some subsets are provably non-measurable.
Because computing probabilities on every subset is too slow for real-time trading systems.
Because the real line has too many points, so we only need the Borel sets to keep the data files small.
Because regulators require a named sigma-algebra on all model documentation.
scenarios.why: Probability's axioms (nonnegativity, normalization, countable additivity) only make sense on a collection of sets closed under the operations the axioms use: complements and countable unions. On the continuum, assigning a consistent probability to literally every subset is impossible — there exist non-measurable sets — so measure theory restricts probability to a sigma-algebra, typically the Borel sets, where the axioms hold.
scenarios.hint: Which axiom of probability needs you to take a countable union of events?

scenarios.title: Expectation as integral
scenarios.situation: A desk quant prices a simple contract that pays $10 if a coin lands heads and $0 if tails, repeated many times. A new hire computes the 'average payout' as (10 + 0) / 2 = $5 and asks why the probability course keeps insisting expectation is 'integration with respect to a probability measure.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the measure-theoretic view of expectation, in plain terms?
choices: Expectation is the integral of the random variable (a measurable function from the sample space to the reals) with respect to the probability measure: E[X] = integral X dP — the weighted average over outcomes, which reduces to a sum for discrete variables and a density-weighted integral for continuous ones.
Expectation is the median of the distribution, computed by integrating the CDF from 0 to 1.
Expectation only applies to discrete variables; continuous ones use the mode instead.
Expectation is defined by Monte Carlo simulation, so no closed form is ever needed.
scenarios.why: Viewing X as a measurable function and E[X] as its integral against P unifies the discrete sum and the continuous density integral into one definition — and it is the definition that lets you prove the theorems quants rely on, like linearity of expectation and dominated convergence, without re-proving them for each distribution family.
scenarios.hint: What does X as a function map FROM and TO?

scenarios.title: The absorbing Markov chain
scenarios.situation: A credit-risk model tracks a bond's rating each quarter as a Markov chain over states {A, B, Default}, where Default is absorbing (once defaulted, the bond stays defaulted). The risk team needs the probability that a currently A-rated bond eventually defaults — not the probability after exactly N quarters, but ever.
scenarios.prompt: How do you compute the eventual-default probability from state A?
choices: Solve the first-step equations: let h_A, h_B be the eventual-default probabilities; then h_A = p_AA*h_A + p_AB*h_B + p_ADefault*1 and h_B = p_BA*h_A + p_BB*h_B + p_BDefault*1, and solve the linear system for h_A (with h_Default = 1).
Raise the transition matrix to the 4th power and read off the entry for (A, Default).
Compute the stationary distribution of the chain and take the Default component.
Simulate one path of the chain for 100 steps and use its endpoint.
scenarios.why: First-step analysis conditions on the first transition and writes the absorption probability as a weighted average of the same quantity from the successor states, yielding a linear system. This is exact for eventual absorption, unlike a fixed-horizon power (which truncates the tail) or the stationary distribution (which here is degenerate at the absorbing state and carries no information about where the chain started).
scenarios.hint: Write the equation for h_A by conditioning on the first step.

scenarios.title: Discounting the cash flow
scenarios.situation: A hiring committee interviews you for a quant-adjacent role and hands you a warm-up: a project pays $110 in one year and $121 in two years. The risk-free rate is 10% per year, compounded annually. They ask what the project is worth today and whether you'd pay $195 for it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct present value, and the decision?
choices: PV = 110/1.1 + 121/1.1^2 = 100 + 100 = $200, so paying $195 is a $5 positive-NPV deal — take it.
PV = 110 + 121 = $231 discounted by 10% once = $210; take it.
scenarios.why: Each cash flow is discounted by the number of periods until it arrives: 110/1.1 = 100 and 121/1.21 = 100, so PV = $200. NPV = 200 − 195 = +$5 > 0, so the investment creates value. The common traps are discounting the two-year flow by only one year, or discounting the total by a single factor.
scenarios.hint: How many years until the $121 arrives?

scenarios.title: Why Brownian motion?
scenarios.situation: A researcher proposes modeling a stock price as a random walk with fixed-size steps each minute. A senior quant rejects it and says the desk standard is geometric Brownian motion: dS = mu*S*dt + sigma*S*dW. The researcher asks what specifically Brownian motion buys them that the fixed-step walk doesn't.
scenarios.prompt: What is the essential mathematical property of Brownian motion that makes it the standard driver?
choices: Brownian motion has continuous paths with independent, stationary, normally distributed increments — the continuous-time limit of the random walk — and the geometric form (scaling the noise by the price S) keeps prices positive and produces log-normal returns, matching the multiplicative nature of compounding.
Brownian motion guarantees the price never goes negative because the steps shrink over time.
Brownian motion is used because its increments are predictable one step ahead, which makes hedging exact.
Brownian motion was chosen historically and any symmetric process would price options identically.
scenarios.why: Brownian motion is the scaling limit of the simple random walk (Donsker's theorem): continuous paths, independent increments, W_t − W_s ~ N(0, t−s). Geometric Brownian motion multiplies that noise by the price level, so returns — not absolute moves — are normal, prices stay positive, and compounding is multiplicative. The fixed-step walk is the discrete skeleton; Brownian motion is its continuous-time limit, which is what makes stochastic calculus (Ito's lemma) applicable.
scenarios.hint: If you shrink the step size and speed up the steps, what does the random walk converge to?

scenarios.title: The one-step binomial
scenarios.situation: A stock trades at $100. In one period it moves to $110 (up) or $90 (down). The risk-free rate is 5% per period. You must price a European call with strike $100 expiring in one period. A colleague prices it as the 'expected payoff' using the real-world 50/50 probabilities: 0.5*10 + 0.5*0 = $5, discounted to $4.76.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct arbitrage-free price?
choices: About $7.14: the risk-neutral probability is p = (1.05x100 - 90)/(110 - 90) = 0.75, so the call value is (0.75x10 + 0.25x0)/1.05 = 7.5/1.05 = $7.14 — exactly the cost of the replicating portfolio (delta = 0.5 shares), which is why no other price is arbitrage-free.
The colleague is right: $4.76, since expected payoff under 50/50 is the fair price.
The call is worth $10 because the stock can reach $110.
The call is worth $0 because the down move wipes out the payoff.
scenarios.why: The colleague priced under the real-world measure; arbitrage-free pricing uses the risk-neutral probability that makes the stock's expected growth equal the risk-free rate: p = (R*S − S_down)/(S_up − S_down) = (105 − 90)/20 = 0.75. Then V = (p*10 + (1−p)*0)/1.05 = 7.5/1.05 ≈ $7.14. This is exactly the cost of the replicating portfolio (delta = (10−0)/(110−90) = 0.5 shares), which is why no arbitrage is possible at any other price.
scenarios.hint: What probability makes the stock's expected one-period return exactly the risk-free rate?

lessons.title: Quantitative Finance Mathematics — Core concepts
concepts: A probability space is a triple (Omega, F, P): outcomes, a sigma-algebra F of measurable events closed under complements and countable unions, and a probability measure P assigning each event a number in [0,1] with P(Omega)=1 and countable additivity.

A random variable X is a measurable function from Omega to the reals; expectation E[X] is the Lebesgue integral of X against P — a weighted average that reduces to a sum for discrete X and an integral against a density for continuous X. Linearity, E[aX+bY]=aE[X]+bE[Y], is the workhorse of pricing.

A Markov chain forgets its past: the next state depends only on the current one. Absorbing states, stationary distributions (pi = pi*P), and first-step equations turn 'what happens eventually' into linear algebra.

Brownian motion W_t is the continuous-time limit of the random walk: continuous paths, independent increments, W_t − W_s ~ N(0, t−s). Geometric Brownian motion dS = mu*S*dt + sigma*S*dW models prices with multiplicative, log-normal returns and is the engine inside Black-Scholes.

Money has a time value: PV = CF_t / (1+r)^t. Net present value (NPV) is the decision rule — take positive-NPV projects. Returns, variance, and covariance are the vocabulary of risk: Var and Cov feed directly into portfolio theory.

Discrete-time pricing (the binomial model) prices derivatives by replication: build a portfolio of stock and bond that matches the derivative's payoff in every state, and no-arbitrage forces the derivative's price to equal the portfolio's cost. Risk-neutral probabilities are the bookkeeping that makes this automatic.

example.code:
def binomial_call(S, K, u, d, r, steps=1):
    # One-period (or multi-period) binomial call via risk-neutral pricing
    R = 1 + r
    p = (R - d) / (u - d)          # risk-neutral probability
    from math import comb
    price = 0.0
    for j in range(steps + 1):     # j = number of up moves
        ST = S * (u ** j) * (d ** (steps - j))
        payoff = max(ST - K, 0)
        prob = comb(steps, j) * (p ** j) * ((1 - p) ** (steps - j))
        price += prob * payoff
    return price / (R ** steps)

print(f"{binomial_call(100, 100, 1.1, 0.9, 0.05):.2f}")  # -> 7.14
example.walkthrough: The risk-neutral probability p makes the stock grow at the risk-free rate in expectation. Each terminal node gets its binomial probability under p, its call payoff, and we discount the p-weighted average back at the risk-free rate. The printed 7.14 matches the hand calculation from the scenario — replication and risk-neutral pricing agree.

pitfalls: Common trap: pricing with real-world probabilities. Expected payoff under the physical measure is not the price — arbitrage-free pricing always runs under the risk-neutral measure where every asset grows at the risk-free rate.
Common trap: forgetting that sigma-algebras matter only on uncountable spaces. On a finite sample space you can take the power set; the measurability machinery exists for the continuum.
Common trap: treating Brownian motion increments as predictable. W_t has independent increments — knowing the path so far tells you nothing about the next increment beyond its distribution.
Common trap: discounting a multi-period cash flow by a single factor. Each cash flow is divided by (1+r)^t for its own t — discounting the sum by one factor is the classic NPV error.

labs.title: Verify the binomial pricer by simulation
labs.objective: Write a Python script that prices the one-step binomial call from the lesson both by the closed-form risk-neutral formula and by Monte Carlo under the risk-neutral measure, and confirm the two agree.
steps: Create binom_check.py implementing the risk-neutral formula for S=100, K=100, u=1.1, d=0.9, r=0.05 and printing the closed-form price.
Add a Monte Carlo loop with 200,000 paths under the risk-neutral up-probability p=0.75, discount each terminal payoff at 5%, and print the simulated price.
Run the script and compare the two printed prices — they should agree to about two decimals.
Change the random seed and re-run: confirm the Monte Carlo estimate is stable while the closed form is exact.
Write your one-paragraph conclusion in RESULTS.txt: why agreement between the two methods validates risk-neutral pricing.

checks.hint: Your closed-form price should print approximately 7.14.
Print a labeled Monte Carlo line so the comparison is visible.

labs.title: Brownian motion: verify the scaling law
labs.objective: Simulate Brownian motion paths and verify empirically that increments are normal with variance equal to the time step — the property that makes Brownian motion the limit of the random walk.
steps: Create brownian_check.py that simulates 50,000 paths of Brownian motion on [0,1] using 100 steps each (increments N(0, 1/100)).
Compute the sample variance of W_1 across all paths and print it — theory says Var(W_1) = 1.
Compute the sample variance of a single mid-path increment (e.g., W_0.5 − W_0.49) and print it — theory says 0.01.
Verify independence: print the sample correlation between two non-overlapping increments — it should be near zero.
Record all three statistics in RESULTS.txt with the theoretical value beside each.

checks.hint: Label your printed statistics so the check can find them.
Print the word 'correlation' with the increment-correlation value.

behavioral.prompt: Explain a sigma-algebra to a portfolio manager with no math background, in under two minutes.
behavioral.framework: ELI5-then-formal: plain analogy first, precise definition second, one-line payoff.
points: Open with the analogy: the list of questions the model is allowed to ask — you can't assign odds to a question you can't even state
Name the closure properties in plain words: if you can ask it, you can ask its opposite and any countable combination
Close with why it matters to them: it guarantees the probabilities your risk numbers rest on are self-consistent
pitfalls: Reciting the textbook definition without the analogy
Claiming it matters for finite coin-flip models (it doesn't — it matters on the continuum)
Going past two minutes

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you caught an error in a model or a calculation before it caused damage.
points: Set the stakes: what the model was deciding and who relied on it
Show the detection method: the sanity check, unit test, or hand calculation that flagged it
Quantify the avoided damage and name the process change you made so it can't recur
pitfalls: Picking a trivial typo with no stakes
Taking sole credit when it was a team catch
No lesson or process change at the end

behavioral.prompt: Why does risk-neutral pricing work? Convince me it's not just a mathematical trick.
behavioral.framework: Intuition-first: replication story, then the formula, then the no-arbitrage punchline.
points: Start with replication: the price equals the cost of the stock-and-bond portfolio that reproduces the payoff in every state
Explain risk-neutral probabilities as bookkeeping that prices that replicating portfolio automatically
Land on no-arbitrage: any other price lets someone lock in a risk-free profit, so the market can't sustain it
pitfalls: Saying 'because the math says so'
Confusing risk-neutral with risk-free or with real-world probabilities
Forgetting the replication argument entirely

behavioral.prompt: Describe the hardest mathematical concept you've had to learn for quant work and how you mastered it.
points: Name the concept and why it resisted you (the specific confusion, not 'it was hard')
Show the method: the textbook, the worked examples, the code you wrote to make it concrete
Prove mastery: the problem you can now solve that you couldn't before
pitfalls: Choosing something you never actually struggled with
Listing resources without showing the work
No proof of current competence

behavioral.prompt: A trader says your model's assumption is wrong. Walk me through how you respond.
points: Show you listen first: restate their objection to confirm you understand the market intuition behind it
Describe verification: which diagnostic or backtest you'd run to check who's right
Explain the decision rule: when you'd change the model vs. defend the assumption, and how you'd communicate either
pitfalls: Getting defensive about the model
Caving immediately without checking
No mention of evidence or testing

behavioral.prompt: Explain Brownian motion and why quants use it, to a smart intern.
behavioral.framework: Build-up: random walk, take the limit, state the properties, name the payoff.
points: Start with the coin-flip random walk they already know
Take the continuous limit: smaller steps, faster flipping — paths become continuous but jagged everywhere
State the two properties that matter: independent increments and normal scaling with time; note geometric BM keeps prices positive
pitfalls: Leading with the SDE before the intuition
Claiming Brownian paths are smooth or predictable
Skipping why geometric (multiplicative) fits prices better than arithmetic

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time a simulation or backtest misled you, and what you changed.
points: Describe the misleading result and what you initially concluded
Name the flaw: look-ahead bias, insufficient paths, wrong measure, seed dependence
Show the fix and the validation you added — the check that now catches it
pitfalls: Blaming the data without owning the design flaw
No concrete validation added afterward
A story where nothing was actually at stake

behavioral.prompt: Where does this 30-hour path leave you, and what is your next step toward quant readiness?
points: Name what you can now do: price discrete models, reason about stochastic processes, read quant papers' probability language
Name the gap honestly: continuous-time stochastic calculus (Ito's lemma) is the next layer, covered in the Quant Ladder path
State the concrete next action with a timeline
pitfalls: Claiming you're job-ready as a quant researcher from one foundations module
No named next step
Vague 'keep learning' without a plan

sections.heading: Probability essentials
items: Probability space: (Omega, F, P); F a sigma-algebra, P a probability measure
E[X] = integral X dP; linearity: E[aX+bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y]
Var(X) = E[X^2] − E[X]^2; Cov(X,Y) = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y]
Markov property: P(X_{n+1} | history) = P(X_{n+1} | X_n); stationary pi satisfies pi = pi P

sections.heading: Stochastic processes
items: Brownian motion: W_0=0, continuous paths, independent increments, W_t − W_s ~ N(0, t−s)
Geometric BM: dS = mu S dt + sigma S dW; S_t log-normal
Random walk -> Brownian motion in the scaling limit

sections.heading: Financial math
items: PV = CF_t / (1+r)^t; NPV = sum PV − cost; take NPV > 0
One-period return: (P_1 − P_0)/P_0; log return: ln(P_1/P_0)
Binomial risk-neutral p = (R − d)/(u − d); price = E_Q[payoff] / R

glossary.def: A collection of subsets of the sample space closed under complements and countable unions — the events probability is allowed to talk about.
A measurable function from the sample space to the real numbers; the bridge between outcomes and numbers.
The integral of a random variable with respect to the probability measure — the probability-weighted average.
A stochastic process where the future depends only on the present state, not the history.
A continuous-time stochastic process with continuous paths and independent, normally distributed increments; the scaling limit of the random walk.
The standard stock-price model: dS = mu S dt + sigma S dW, giving positive prices and log-normal returns.
The probability measure under which every asset grows at the risk-free rate in expectation; the measure used for arbitrage-free pricing.
The sum of discounted future cash flows minus the initial cost; the decision rule is to take positive-NPV projects.

checklist: Can state the three components of a probability space and why the sigma-algebra is needed
Can compute expectation, variance, and covariance from first principles
Can set up and solve first-step equations for an absorbing Markov chain
Can discount a cash-flow stream and make an NPV decision
Can derive the one-step binomial price and the risk-neutral probability by hand
Can explain why geometric Brownian motion — not the fixed-step walk — is the desk standard
